name: Ngatyi / Rainbow Serpent traditions
tradition: Multiple Aboriginal Australian creation and Country traditions
candidate_type: ancestral being / creation narrative / water-and-Country tradition

discovery.summary: Australian Museum material records Barkandji knowledge in which Ngatyi are ancestral creator beings associated with Country, waterways, rain, protection, and places requiring respectful avoidance; the museum also notes that Rainbow Serpent traditions occur in many parts of Australia but vary by community. National Museum of Australia material likewise documents distinct regional Rainbow Snake/Serpent traditions, including Bardi and Djawi and Kimberley examples. Source basis: Australian Museum, 'Save our Ngatyi (Rainbow Serpents)' and 'Indigenous Australians: Australia’s First Peoples'; National Museum of Australia, 'Kimberley, Western Australia'.
discovery.why_relevant: This is a high-value provenance candidate because it demonstrates why MFTL must not collapse similarly named Indigenous traditions into a single pan-Australian myth. It can later support community-specific entities, creation claims, water-place relations, ritual restrictions, and transmission records while preserving cultural boundaries and restricted-knowledge cautions.

sources.title: Save our Ngatyi (Rainbow Serpents)
sources.source_type: museum / First Nations knowledge and collection record
sources.notes: Australian Museum page presenting Barkandji artist and elder Badger Bates's account of Ngatyi, including creator/water associations, continuing respect, and place-specific restrictions.

sources.title: Indigenous Australians: Australia’s First Peoples exhibition 1996-2015
sources.notes: Provides broader museum context for Rainbow Serpent themes, watercourse associations, landscape-creation narratives, destructive/protective aspects, and the warning that some story aspects are restricted.

sources.title: Kimberley, Western Australia
sources.notes: Documents regional Rainbow Snake traditions and emphasizes that rainbow snakes/serpents feature in creation stories of many Australian regions rather than constituting one uniform narrative.

notes: Canonicalization must be community- and source-specific. Do not treat 'Rainbow Serpent' as one universal Aboriginal Australian doctrine, and do not reproduce culturally restricted material beyond what authorized institutional/community sources make public. No theological assessment has been made.
